solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: When skin turns numb

indicators.note: a thing that turns round faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: 'as' can mean 'when', as in 'as I left'
peel is the skin of a fruit

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding observation about when skin loses its feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin turns numb' reads as one statement, but 'turns' only flips the word for skin, and 'numb' stands alone at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb that has gone to sleep has lost all feeling, so the word describes a numb arm or foot.

clue.text: One over the limit cabby makes take a shot?

definitions.text: One over the limit cabby makes take a shot?

blocks.clueFragment: One over the limit cabby makes take a shot?
blocks.note: surface reading: a drunk taxi driver forcing someone to down a shot of spirits

blocks.clueFragment: One over the limit cabby makes take a shot?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a roadside device that a speeding taxi driver causes to take a photograph

explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the limit' suggests drink-driving and 'shot' a measure of spirits; here the limit is the speed limit and the shot is a photograph, and the grammar is the thing the cabby makes take a shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Roadside enforcement devices photograph vehicles travelling faster than the posted legal maximum, triggered by the offending driver.

clue.text: Invest in nurse given what is owed

blocks.note: EN is an Enrolled Nurse
what is due is what is owed

explanation.surface: Advice to put money into a nurse's pay to settle a debt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invest in' looks like a financial phrase, but 'Invest' alone is the definition, in its old sense of clothing or endowing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest someone with a quality or office is to endow or furnish them with it, an older literary synonym.

clue.text: Sketch liberal found in offensive, juvenile annual?

indicators.note: something found in another sits inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a plan is a sketch or outline drawing
L is the abbreviation for Liberal
the Tet Offensive of 1968 in the Vietnam War

explanation.surface: A cartoon about a liberal tucked inside a rude children's yearbook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annual' suggests a children's yearbook, but it is a plant that lives one year; the question mark flags that a young annual is only one kind of young plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A small young plant, especially one produced by a parent plant, is a juvenile, and an annual is one kind of plant.

clue.text: Devout person gets garment for flasher

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for saint, a devout person
a robe is a long garment

explanation.surface: A pious person hands a coat to an indecent exposer to cover up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the flasher a man in a raincoat; the definition means a light that flashes.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapidly flashing lamp used in discos and photography is literally a thing that flashes.

clue.text: Place in which empty-bellied piper gets a brownie?

indicators.note: an empty belly has nothing in its middle, so only the outside letters are kept
'in which' says that something sits within what came before, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a site is a place
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A hungry bagpiper is rewarded with a chocolate brownie somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A brownie is not the cake here but a helpful household goblin from Scottish folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore a brownie is a small mischievous domestic elf, one kind of fairy or supernatural spirit.

clue.text: A way you could describe Five Children and It?

definitions.text: A way you could describe Five Children and It?

blocks.clueFragment: A way you could describe Five Children and It?
blocks.note: surface reading: how to summarise E. Nesbit's children's novel Five Children and It
setter's reading: children are family members, and 'it' is slang for sex, so both can be called by one word

explanation.walkthrough: Five Children and It is a 1902 children's novel by E. Nesbit. The answer also means narrations or accounts, which is how a book might be described.
explanation.definitionFit: Children are kin, sex is described by this plural noun, and accounts of events are also given this name.

clue.text: Work bishop gets around Slough

indicators.note: going around means turning back on yourself, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: to go is to work or function
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop's job takes him round the town of Slough.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough, capitalised, looks like the town west of London; it is the ordinary word for a swamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A slough is a swamp or marshy hollow, and a bog is wet spongy ground of the same kind.

clue.text: Curt Irish cops ruined festival

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked out of its proper shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Brusque Irish police spoiled a local festival.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole answer is made from the first three words; Corpus Christi is a Christian feast honouring the Eucharist.
explanation.definitionFit: This Catholic feast day celebrating the body of Christ falls in early summer and is marked with processions.

clue.text: Try and stop E and smack when out of head

indicators.note: out of head means without its head, so the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: to end something is to stop it
taken as written
a smack is a taste or flavour, as in 'a smack of garlic'

explanation.surface: A plea to quit ecstasy and heroin when off one's head.
explanation.walkthrough: E is slang for ecstasy and smack for heroin, and 'out of head' sounds like intoxication; really smack means a taste and loses its head.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to try hard at something is to make an earnest attempt or effort.

clue.text: Screamed command to get off the blocks?

indicators.note: a scream is spoken out loud, so we go by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: 'Leggo!' is a slurred 'let go!', an order to get off

explanation.surface: Someone yells at a person to get off something.
explanation.walkthrough: A deliberately groan-worthy pun: the toy name is said like the shouted slurred order. 'Off the blocks' suggests a sprint start, but the blocks are the toy bricks.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish brand of interlocking plastic toy bricks is the best known set of building blocks for children.

clue.text: Lawyer backing green bill

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so these letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: a DA is a US District Attorney
vert is green in heraldry

explanation.surface: An attorney supports environmental legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green bill' looks like environmental law or a banknote; the bill is a printed notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a printed poster or handbill promoting something, which is a piece of publicity.

clue.text: Top tips to play second breaks of service

indicators.note: to play with something is to toy with it and move it around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Coaching advice on how to break serve in tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks of service' suggests tennis, but the service is a racing car's tyre change and refuelling.
explanation.definitionFit: In motor racing, cars pause in the pits for refuelling and tyre changes, brief halts for servicing.

clue.text: Lassie heads for Spooner’s doorway

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts are exchanged

blocks.note: a lassie is a girl, so girly, and pates are heads; swap the opening sounds G and P

explanation.surface: The famous film collie leads the way through a door.
explanation.walkthrough: Lassie is the TV collie but here just a girl; swapping the first sounds of the two words produces the entrance to heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: In popular tradition the entrance to heaven, guarded by St Peter, is a gate made of pearl.

clue.text: Organ Saracen moved with foremost of props

indicators.note: things moved are shifted from their places, so the letters are rearranged
the foremost part of a word is its very front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A rugby scene: Saracens is a London rugby club and props are front-row forwards, so a Saracens player shifts alongside the props.
explanation.walkthrough: Saracens is an English rugby union club and a prop is a front-row forward; the rugby picture hides an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The gland behind the stomach producing insulin and digestive enzymes is an internal body organ.

clue.text: Force prisoners on to coach

blocks.note: cons are convicts
to train someone is to coach them

explanation.surface: Convicts are compelled to board a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like a bus the prisoners are forced onto; it is the verb meaning instruct.
explanation.definitionFit: To constrain someone is to compel or oblige them, a close synonym of forcing them.

clue.text: Working sailor came about to enter port

indicators.note: a ship that comes about turns onto the opposite tack, so the letters face the other way
to enter is to go inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working
AB is an able-bodied seaman

explanation.surface: A seaman on duty tacks round to sail into harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The sailing phrase 'came about' fits the nautical surface but is the turnaround signal. Oban is a ferry port on the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: This west Highland town is a harbour serving ferries to the Hebridean islands, so it is a seaport.

clue.text: Short story one acted out

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A brief tale that a person performed on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acted out' reads as a single phrase meaning performed, but 'acted' belongs with the fodder and only 'out' signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief amusing account of a real incident is a small spoken tale.

clue.text: List articles for foreign and domestic markets

blocks.note: le is a French definite article, one for a foreign market
an is an English indefinite article, one for the home market

explanation.surface: An inventory of goods to be sold at home and abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'List' looks like a noun for an inventory; it is the verb for a ship tilting.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship that lists tilts to one side, and to tilt or incline is the verb meaning slope.

clue.text: Truly divine nursing home in the sticks?

indicators.note: to nurse something is to hold it close, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: holy means divine or sacred
a bird's home built in the twigs

explanation.surface: A really heavenly care home out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the sticks' suggests the remote countryside and 'nursing home' a care home; the home is a bird's, made of sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adverbs express sincerity, as in 'honestly, I mean it' or 'truly, I mean it'.

clue.text: Repeated slogan one in Labour facility sent up

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a man is one member of the labour force, a worker
an art is a facility or skill

explanation.surface: A Labour party catchphrase about a facility gets mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised Labour suggests the political party, but it means the workforce; 'sent up' suggests mockery but just turns the facility upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or phrase chanted over and over, or a much-repeated catchphrase, is called by this Sanskrit-derived term.

clue.text: Seasoned beef done with Smash is half-finished

indicators.note: half of the word is finished and gone, so only its front half is kept

blocks.note: something done is over and past
to ram is to smash into
the first of its two letters

explanation.surface: A meal of beef and Smash, the instant mashed potato brand, is half cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: Smash is a British brand of instant mashed potato, which suits the dinner picture; here it is the verb meaning crash into.
explanation.definitionFit: This smoked, spiced and cured cut of brisket is a deli staple, beef that has been heavily seasoned.

clue.text: In attack, coppers possibly traded knight for rook

indicators.note: trading one thing for another swaps them, so one letter replaces another

blocks.note: coppers are low-value coins, an example of small change
N is the chess notation for knight
R is the chess notation for rook

explanation.surface: A chess attack in which police officers swapped pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: Coppers are police officers in the surface, but here they are copper coins; 'possibly' marks them as one example of loose coins.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is a sudden headlong rush at an enemy, an assault or offensive.

clue.text: Is your setter on leave in China?

blocks.note: the setter speaking of themself says 'am I'
to go is to leave

explanation.surface: The setter wonders whether they are holidaying in China.
explanation.walkthrough: China is not the country: in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' means mate, a friend. 'Your setter' is the setter talking about themself, so 'is your setter' becomes 'am I'.
explanation.definitionFit: Via rhyming slang a china is a pal, and the Spanish word for a friend is borrowed into English.

clue.text: Iron put over large and a small jumper

indicators.note: something put over another covers it on both sides, so it surrounds the other piece

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
L is the abbreviation for large
taken as written

explanation.surface: Pressing clothes: ironing a large sweater and a small one.
explanation.walkthrough: Jumper is British for a sweater, which suits the ironing picture; here it is something that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny wingless parasitic insect is famous for leaping huge distances relative to its size.

clue.text: One raised by wolves about to go in lake, say

definitions.text: One raised by wolves about to go

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for lake
e.g. means 'for example', as does 'say'

explanation.surface: A child brought up by wolves, like Mowgli, is about to jump into a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a comic picture: a wolf, like a dog, cocks a limb when it is about to go, that is, to urinate. 'Raised by wolves' wants to mean brought up by them.
explanation.definitionFit: Canines lift a hind limb to urinate, so this limb is the thing a wolf raises before relieving itself.

clue.text: One who gets under your skin at work?

definitions.text: One who gets under your skin at work?

blocks.clueFragment: One who gets under your skin at work?
blocks.note: surface reading: an irritating colleague in the office
setter's reading: someone whose job is literally inserting ink beneath the skin

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets under your skin' is an idiom for annoying someone; taken literally it describes a needle putting ink into the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Body artists inject ink into the dermis with needles, so their work literally goes beneath the skin.

clue.text: You horse around with lawyer in a state

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: U is text-speak for you
a nag is an old horse
a DA is a US District Attorney

explanation.surface: Someone fooling about with their solicitor is in a right state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' reads as 'upset', but 'a state' is the definition, a country in East Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: The East African republic is a sovereign nation, and a nation is a state.

clue.text: First? I will occupy that position!

definitions.text: First? I will occupy that position!

indicators.note: occupying a position means taking the place of whatever was there, so one part replaces another

blocks.note: the ego is the I, the self
written 1ST; the numeral 1 is the position to be filled

explanation.surface: A self-centred person claims first place for themself.
explanation.walkthrough: Write 'first' as 1ST, then put the self, the ego, in place of the 1. The whole clue is also what a self-centred person would say.
explanation.definitionFit: A selfish person always puts themself in first place, which is the whole clue's boast.
